utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is the case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we hear the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? I see none, so we could have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva, we have some problem with the pictures the witness drew yesterday, so will you please do it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness H.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to have to trouble you again with the photograph that you marked yesterday, it wasn't -- your markings weren't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So could photograph P360 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you have that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please circle the building where the command -- battalion command was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you write the letter C there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask the witness to mark on this photograph again. I can do it on a different one or I can keep that photograph there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to save the space for more evidence in the future, I think you could do it on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness H, yesterday before we broke, I asked you about the village of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Court, were you involved in any military action at Uzdol in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On what date did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your military action at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: To destroy a tank that was positioned next to the school building, the adjacent artillery, and to free up prisoners who had fallen into the hands of the HVO and were being kept inside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well you've almost answered my next question, but under whose control was Uzdol and the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under the HVO's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Apart from the tank which you said was near the school, what other HVO military installations were by the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the military installations, what else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were there soldiers in the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you aware as to how many soldiers there might have been in that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did your military operation involve solely the school or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Solely the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, who told you to go and attack the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I received an assignment from Pero Mustafa [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who was Pero, Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was Enver Buza's deputy, and Enver Buza was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did Enver Buza talk to you about this operation at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where did you speak to Mustafa Hero about your operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him near the village of Here the night before we started out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now the day before the 14th September, 13th, were you in Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did anybody outside of the Prozor Independent Battalion come and visit the command centre in Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did anybody who was not from the Prozor Independent Battalion come to the command centre in Dobro Polje on the 13th September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Halilovic outside the building on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you see Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around noon on the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How did you know it was Mr. Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with this gentleman from the printed media and from various photographs. Then after he'd left, some soldiers came up and told me that Mr. Halilovic had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What was Mr. Halilovic doing in Dobro Polje that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, there were soldiers there lined up outside the command, and Mr. Halilovic spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you lined up with the soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived later. I wasn't there at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court after how long did you join the line-up from when it started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 20 or 25 minutes later, but I can't be very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you joined the line-up, what was Mr. Halilovic doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was addressing the troops. He was giving a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was he there by himself or was he with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Buza was standing near him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, from the time you joined the line-up, did Mr. Buza say anything to the troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Halilovic was giving a speech. What do you recall he said to the soldiers when you were in the line-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, I remember that Mr. Halilovic asked us whether we had enough to eat, whether we had sufficient equipment, whether it was all in good order, whether we had enough footwear, clothes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall him talking about anything else to the troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the soldiers in the line-up asking any questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What was your understanding as to Mr. Halilovic's rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really know exactly what his rank was, but I was aware of the fact that he was a highly-positioned BH army officer. Specifically, I was not aware of his duty or rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, during your time at the Prozor Independent Battalion, did Commander Buza ever line up the soldiers and address you that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know who Salko Gusic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the name rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say "the name rings a bell"; what does it tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is familiar, but I never saw the person. I've no idea who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During your time at the Prozor Independent Battalion, do you recall any other high-ranking military officer addressing the troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, after the line-up with Mr. Halilovic, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he finished speaking, I went to see an officer; he was manning the checkpoint at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did this officer say to you if he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which officer do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The officer who was managing the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that some high-ranking officers had arrived. That was all he said. That was all he told me about these high-ranking officers having arrived, but that was before I joined the line-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: All right. On the day of the line-up, after that, did you leave Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went near the village of Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who told you to go to Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Buza did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to join my group, go to Here, and that we would be receiving further instructions once there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be cautious, I'd like to ask a question of the witness but in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long did it take you to go from Dobro Polje to Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour, an hour and a half; we walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you arrived in Here, can you tell the Court roughly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was it dark or light outside when you arrived in Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark. It was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that when you -- you were told by Buza that when you got to Here you would received further instructions. Did you receive further instructions when you arrived in Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who gave you those instructions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me my task was to join the remaining groups and to attack the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did he tell you how you were supposed to advance on the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many soldiers in your group were going to attack the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall the route you took from Here to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I show the witness photograph 0402-0910?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the previous evidence, are you going to use it again or could we give a number now to that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you are not going to use it again, maybe we could have it admitted into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually if the photograph is on the screen, I will ask that particular question and then we can end with that in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that picture is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I apologise Witness H. I'm just going to take you back briefly. Do you have the same photograph on your screen with the battalion command building in Dobro Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see on that photograph where you were in the line-up when Mr. Halilovic addressed the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean before I joined the line-up or while I was in the line-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: While you were in the line-up -- well, first of all, do you see that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you then mark it with the letter L, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P360.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, just last question about that line-up. To your knowledge, how long did Mr. Halilovic address the troops for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about half an hour, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: All right. May the photograph 0402-0910 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 361.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, do you see a new photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see the village of Here there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark that, please, or if you can, place a circle around the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Here you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, or perhaps just put the letter H on the side of where the village is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you also see in that photograph the school where your group was -- were going to attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please circle that and put the letter S by the side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, if you can, I'd like you to use the pen, and using a dotted line draw on the photograph the route your group took to advance on the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, in taking that route, did you go through any villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers en route to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians en route to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to say roughly what time you set off for the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- not that, but I remember more or less of when it was that we arrived at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at dawn, at the crack of dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, might that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit 361, and the original Prosecution Exhibit 360 -- 361.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that you -- well, the purpose of your attack on the school was to destroy a tank there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why were you told to destroy the tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply that tank was harassing our units and it shelled them daily; it shelled the village of Here every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How far, as the crow flies, was Here from the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but perhaps it was between 800 or 900 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you got to the school just before dawn, tell the Court what happened then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out to attack the school, and at that moment the HVO tank also set out towards the village of Here. We destroyed the tank, and naturally we then engaged in a fight with the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where were the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers were at the school, in the school. And when we attacked the school, another group of the soldiers immediately appeared from the direction of this village, which is below the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that its name is Donja Vast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm going to ask you to point out on the same photograph the direction from where the soldiers came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Might that photograph 0402-0910 -- excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 362.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: My mistake. Might Exhibit 298 be shown to the witness. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, do you see the school there in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please place an S on top of that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see in that photograph where the HVO tank was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark that position with a T, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot mark it with precision, but within a couple of metres I can mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's fine. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said that reinforcements came --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- HVO reinforcements came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Using an arrow, can you indicate their direction, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to say roughly how many soldiers came from that direction as reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really able to say that. Roughly speaking, I think they were the strength of a squad or a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which is roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 to 15 soldiers, possibly 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see on that photograph the village of Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please mark that with the letter H.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you -- if you can say, were you involved in combat at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time, the exact duration. I do not remember how long it was that we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, can you give a rough estimate? Was it half a day? Was it a day? Was it a couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my rough estimate will be that we stayed there between 40 and 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: After the combat, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then we continued to retreat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In which direction did you retreat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, was retreating in the direction of the village of Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able, on the photograph in front of you, to mark the route you took while you were retreating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just some of it because we retreated in fear and in panic so that I cannot really exactly recall the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's fine. Please do what you can on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: While you were retreating, did you come across any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you come across any civilians --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, might that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P363.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that your group took this route that you indicated on the photograph to the school. Were other members of the Prozor Independent Battalion involved in this operation in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did they take a different route to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many of these -- how many members of the Prozor Independent Battalion were involved in this operation in Uzdol, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this direction, the axis which was the one towards the school, there was about 15 or 20 soldiers as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say "in this direction." Do you know of another direction which soldiers would have advanced on the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: After the 14th of September, 1993, were you involved in another attack in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was the attack in Uzdol that you were involved in on the 14th the only attack on Uzdol that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And we object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why? What's the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the order -- or rather, the documents which my learned colleague from the Prosecution intends to show to this witness has already been shown to him during proofing, and this witness has made it very clear that he had never seen the document, didn't know about it, and he was invited by the Prosecution to make assumptions in relation to that document. There's no suggestion on the part of the Prosecutor that this person is an expert in those matters, and as a matter of fact, he is not. So we believe and we submit that this witness should not be shown that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the best way is to have what you said in the record. By doing so, we could show this document to this witness so everything will be clear in the record. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the benefit of my colleague, my questions should reveal the reasons why I want to show this document to Witness H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes. You mean your question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Does the witness have the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see in the middle of that screen, the middle of the document where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we object again. We think that the Prosecution should start with asking the very question as to whether he had seen that document before or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we need some foundation questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not contesting the fact that the witness has not seen the document; I'm simply referring the witness to a portion of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's have it in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, other than witness preparation, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd again like to take you to the paragraph in the middle of the document where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object again for the reason given previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we haven't heard a question yet. I believe that since this document is used and we should allow the Prosecution to put their question clearly in the record. The witness may not have seen this document before but the contents may be something that he's familiar. I don't know myself because I haven't seen -- I don't know whether the document has seen -- this witness has seen this document or not, but anyway we'll see how the witness could answer the questions put by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, in that paragraph, do you see where it reads, "In a comprehensive operation, break the HVO," Croatian Defence Council, "and HV Croatian army forces in the area of Crni Vrh, Uzdol village, Jurici village, and so on." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There is a paragraph which has the word "task" at the side. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right. Now in that paragraph, there is a sentence - and I'm not going to start from the beginning - but it reads, "In a comprehensive operation, breakup the HVO, HV forces in the area of Crni Vrh, Uzdol village, Jurici village, Diva [phoen] village and so on." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see where it's written "Uzdol village"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to ask you, the operation that you were involved in at the school in Uzdol, in your view, is that consistent with a comprehensive operation to breakup the HVO forces in Uzdol village?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we object to this question. It requires some assumptions to be made by the witness, as was done in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could judge from the answer of this witness to see whether it's an assumption or not. You may proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, do you want me to ask the question again or ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As regards this order and the task which I was executing, I fail to see. This is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me put it another way. As a soldier that participated in the military operation at the school in Uzdol, could the ABiH -- or could the Prozor Independent Battalion have taken the village without taking the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the school is also in the village of Uzdol, so I don't see how that could have been one without the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we may have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps before we do, we have identified what we believe to be a slight mistake in the transcript in relation to the name of one individual which was referred at page 3, line 21, that's the man believed to be the deputy commander of Mr. Buza and the transcript refers to this person as "Mustafa Pero." And my colleague I think corrected it himself as being Mustafa Hero, and perhaps the matter could be clarified by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, do you agree on that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I believe that during the break, the transcript could be corrected. Well, we will take our break, and we will resume at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that there is something to submit from the Prosecution side. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. Your honour, we have two motions. The first is a motion for protective measures for the next witness. May we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution here makes their application to drop witness Bahrudin Comor. The Prosecution no longer intends to call him to testify before this Court, and this is a witness which was going to testify this week. Your Honour, depending on what the reaction of the Defence counsel is, I would be very happy to assist the Court with any reasons, but unless I'm invited to do so I will say this for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my friend should treat it as one that's strongly opposed, an order put before the Tribunal, the reasons for what is being proposed. And we've got a fairly substantial response that we want to make to this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The reasons -- this witness was proofed in the last couple of days, and after this witness had been proofed it was the position of the Prosecution that it cannot assist the Prosecution case or indeed assist the Trial Chamber in respect of this case. The reason is, Your Honour, this was a military prosecutor, but during the relevant time that this indictment refers to, he was not a military prosecutor at that time. He started in November of 1993. Your Honour, trials at the ICTY are essentially adversarial, each party may whichever witnesses they wish to prove their case. It is the case that before the trial starts we have to give witness lists, and that is more for the trial management of this case. If we want to add a witness, Your Honour, no doubt the Prosecutor would have to advance cogent reasons as to why we want to add witnesses. But it is our position that if we want to drop a witness from our witness list, we do not have to advance reasons as to why we want to drop a particular witness other than to say it's not going to assist us and there is no reason to call him and waste this Court's time. Time is being of the essence, Your Honour, and there are times that we have witnesses on our list, and at the time we have them we feel there may be something that they can assist, and mostly it is the investigators in the field who have seen these witnesses. It's only when they come here there are times that when a witness is proofed, we see his evidence and feel that he is not somebody who is -- who can talk about the events and about the circumstances of this case. So, Your Honour, for these reasons, I'm not even sure that the Defence counsel should have -- should have a right to challenge the Prosecution's decision. Each party is entitled to call the witnesses they want to prove their case. I cannot see under what rule that a particular party can be forced to call a witness that it does not wish to. Your Honour, this witness -- the proofing notes have been handed to the Defence. The Defence is entitled to call the witness themselves if they feel that this witness can be of some assistance to them. The proofing notes are fair and transparent. We've said -- we put into the proofing notes everything that the witness added to his statement. Your Honour, for these reasons, we -- that we submit that we should be allowed not to call this witness and remove him from our Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks. Your Honours, the witness will not assist the Prosecution's case; there is absolutely no doubt about that. But my learned friend mentioned that the witness would not assist the Tribunal; that's completely wrong. The Prosecutors have got a duty here: They are ministers of justice and they have a duty to assist the Tribunal to find the truth. True it is that it's an adversarial system here, but in the common law system, which is even more adversarial in nature, the Prosecutor's duty of fairness extends to making available, during the Prosecution's own case, all relevant witnesses. Now, in the case of this particular witness, the chronology is very important. Last year, on the 18th -- I'm going to provide a chronology now because it -- I'm not going to make the allegations or the claims that I propose to make without fully putting this on record and so that the Prosecution has an ample opportunity to respond. Bahrudin Comor was interviewed by Investigator Bernard Brun on the 18th of June, 2004, middle of last year is when this statement was taken of this witness. And at the time that that witness gave his statement it was apparent that he was a military prosecutor, and you can see how that's relevant to the Prosecution case because they want to say that Halilovic should have -- Mr. Halilovic should have taken certain steps and they want to say what steps were open to him to take. So this statement was taken by the Prosecutors at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will slow down, I've been asked to. That was on the 18th of June 2004. For completeness, one week later, on the 25th of June, 2004, a more senior Prosecutor named Ibro Bulic, was also interviewed by the same interviewer, Bernard Brun, and he indicated that he was the deputy prosecutor in Mostar and that he'd heard nothing about this until 1994. So he obviously didn't have anything to say about it at all. But Bahrudin Comor was able to say where he was at the time that he offences took place, and he was able to say what the state of the military justice system was at that time. He was able to say that he was appointed in August or early September, and he was able to say what the state of the court building was like, namely that it was blown up and damaged. He was able to say is that the military prosecutors didn't actually start operating until a later time. Do Your Honours have his statement? Because I can indicate that when you look at the statement, it will be absolutely evident that the Prosecutor's claim that this witness can't assist the Tribunal is a hollow one; of course he can assist the Tribunal. Then, Your Honours, what happened next was the Prosecutors decided that they would wish to add this witness to their witness list, and I make this comment. Times change, don't they, because back in January and December of this -- the Prosecution moved a motion to this Court and asked that he be added to their witness list. And they said, "Bahrudun Comor." And in justification of calling him they said this and asked you to rule in their favour on this basis, which I hasten to say has not changed in the least. Bahrudin Comor was appointed military Prosecutor in Konjic in August, September 1993. He will explain the work of the district military court and its jurisdiction. Your Honours, I pause to say that that's clearly a matter of relevance here. He will state that during his time there, he never saw and dealt with a file or report concerning the crimes in Grabovica and Uzdol, although he did receive an instructions from the president and Delic to clear up all crimes committed in the territory, but not on Grabovica or Uzdol. It was said that it was relevant to paragraphs 23, 33, and 34 of the indictment, and it was said that he'd take two hours in viva voce evidence. Based upon those -- those assurances and those submissions by the Prosecutor, you, the Tribunal, agreed to allow him to be added to the list. Now, at that time, it was quite obvious what his expertise was, what his experience was, and what material -- in what ways he was able to assist the Court. Of course it wasn't known -- or perhaps it wasn't known to the Prosecutor. I don't know what was known to the Prosecutors at that time, but whatever may or may not have been known to them, things changed when the proofing notes happened. And I would hand up copies of the proofing notes, three of them, to the Trial Chamber to assist you in knowing exactly what is happening here and why it is that we suggest the Prosecutor is withdrawing this witness. Could these please be handed up, Mr. Court Deputy, to the Tribunal members.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interject here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We have already supplied the proofing notes to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for indicating that they've been supplied to the Court. Now, in having regard to these proofing notes, you'll see that there's a paragraph here saying that "In my time as Prosecutor" -- sorry perhaps first of all. "In September, October 1993 the court in Konjic was not functioning, military Prosecutor's office did not function at that time. We had a room in an apartment. There was no investigative judge appointed at that time." Now, these things are directly relevant to what it was open to Halilovic or his agent or whoever it was that he assigned the task to, in this case as we know who it is, it's Nomin Jankovic [phoen]. But what was actually open to those people, what steps were open? Now that's clearly centrally, directly relevant to material called by the Prosecutor against Halilovic. To press on he says: "In my time as Prosecutor, I never saw a case signed by a military commander, always by the assistant command commander for military security." Now again it's the Defence case of course that what Sefer Halilovic did was to assign the investigation to military security, the SVB as it's been called in this case. And then a sensible qualification is added that except in cases of desertion, the 6th Corp. commander signed up. Now these are matters that are centrally relevant to the case. They don't help the Prosecution; they're very damaging for the Prosecution, so I agree with my learned friend in that regard. But they're pretty helpful to the Tribunal in my submission, directly helpful. It then goes on to say if -- I just invite you to turn over the page. "With respect to the killings such as Grabovica, my opinion is that Sefer Halilovic had the duty to ask his military security officer to investigate." Now, I just interpose this before I go on. That obviously assumes that Halilovic was in command, and we're not -- for these purposes I'm not going to seek to attack the witness's comments about that. But let it be assumed that he was in command and that the Tribunal made such a finding in a relevant way, of course, not adapted to local laws entirely but to the law that you have to apply, which is -- comes from a different source. But he says: "My opinion is Sefer Halilovic had the duty to ask his military security officer to investigate. Once that's done, that is, asking the military security officer to investigate, then in my view then he would have discharged his responsibility." Now, that opinion is not binding on you, the Tribunal; you will have to assess that for yourselves, of course. But coming from a military prosecutor, that's crucial evidence. Now, in my submission, this situation is totally different to the one that occurred yesterday when the learned Prosecutor sought to withdraw a witness. Yesterday -- I can't recall, Your Honours, if we were in private session yesterday or not when that issue arose as to withdrawing that previous witness, so I'll just speak of it -- I'll keep it in very general terms in any event so hopefully it won't be necessary. When the Prosecutor sought to withdraw the witness yesterday, the Prosecutor didn't at that time assert that there was no need to seek leave of the Tribunal nor seek to say that the Defence shouldn't make any submissions about it. At that time, things proceeded normally and properly. The Prosecutor was placed in a difficult position by that witness, responded entirely appropriately, and met with no quarrels by the Defence, and indeed I think we expressed our gratitude for the way it was handled and it was handled quite properly. It stands in stark contrast to the situation today. There is -- on that occasion -- whatever else may be said of the witness who was withdrawn then, that witness was at the very least conniving in crime, I mean effectively in making the suggestions that were made, and the Prosecutor was actually within her rights to do what she did. But here, there is no suggestion of impropriety, dishonesty, sneakiness, or unreliability, nor is there a suggestion of change in evidence. The evidence is just what it always was. It's just that now that the question comes to be asked: How does it apply to the accused here? The answer is rather a disaster for the Prosecutor. In those circumstances, Your Honour, the Prosecution's application here is, in my submission, not consistent with the Prosecutor's high duties to preserve the fair trial in this Court. A fair trial in this Court is the product not just of a fair bench of Judges but of a Prosecution that runs its case in a fair way, even when evidence does not assist it. Now, that brings to a point the issue of what the Tribunal can do in such a situation. On the one hand, a Tribunal finds itself in an awkward position because although I submit you clearly do have the power to order the Prosecutor to call a witness, how that evolves in reality is very difficult. It cannot be the case in an adversarial system that you can compel the Prosecutors to ask particular questions, nor can you direct the Prosecutor to deal with particular topics. And I do not ask you to do that, and I think in -- a moment's analysis makes it clear that that would be dragging the Tribunal into the arena in a way that you shouldn't be asked to do by the Defence and so I'm not going to ask you to do so. But however, there are two ways in which the Tribunal can assist in this case and, in my submission, do justice in this case. The first is that you can decline to permit the Prosecutor to withdraw this witness. You can't force them to ask questions, but you can decline to let them withdraw the witness. The witness is here. He is not said to be unreliable and plainly has relevant, admissible, and significant evidence to give. In that situation, in common law jurisdictions, it is very frequently done by Prosecutors who have a witness this their hands that they don't like and don't propose to elicit evidence from, to nevertheless call that witness purely to permit the Defence to cross-examine that witness and, in an appropriate case, to let the Court ask whatever questions the Court may chance to have. That's an option that's well and truly open here, and it's the option that the Prosecutor should follow. So my first submission is that the Court decline to allow the Prosecutor to withdraw this witness from the list; that witness should be called. If the Prosecutor declines to ask any questions, that is a matter for the Prosecutor, but I have questions to ask and they are pretty short ones. A second option that's open is that this material go in under 89(F); that would save the time problems that my learned friend has referred to as being of the essence. Of course this statement plus the proofing notes could be tendered; if that was done, I wouldn't cross-examine. And frankly, that is the evidence that we think assists -- those are the questions that -- in the proofing notes that I plainly would have been seeking to elicit from the witness. Now, I should pause to say, again, as I've said before, that we've been critical from time to time about Prosecutors' proofing practices, and the notes provided here under the hand of Mr. Sachdeva are an example of how exactly it should be done. It's quite proper proofing notes, and we are happy with what their contents is. But they're here now. Now this material is capable of bearing on the guilt or otherwise of Mr. Halilovic; it's relevant. Regulation 2 of the Prosecution's own guidelines give -- wish upon them -- or require of them to act as ministers justice and to be, if you like, fair. So my first submission is that you can decline to allow them to withdraw this witness. It's up to them whether they want to ask any questions or not. Secondly, it could be suggested to the Prosecutor by the Bench - if you are persuaded by what I say, of course, after you've looked at the statements the proofing notes - that they might want to reconsider their decision not to call this witness, and that is a matter that would be, in my submission, highly appropriate. The Prosecution should have a think about this. Clearly it is a bad development for them and clearly it would be best for their case if the issue went away, but it may be that some time taken to think about it might bear fruit. If neither of those -- if none of those courses recommended themselves to the Court, then in my submission - and this is something I do very reluctantly because I don't favour the indiscriminate calling of witnesses at all by the Tribunal and I'm sure that the Tribunal would have its own thoughts as to in what circumstances you would want to call a witness, if ever, but this may then turn out to be such a situation. If the Prosecutor persists in refusing to call a witness, this may be one of those rare occasions when the Tribunal, having regard to all of the circumstances, might take the unusual step. It's not a step that I -- well, I've said that already, frankly, Your Honours. So for those reasons, I ask Your Honours to consider those options and the Prosecutor may choose to respond to any of them as they see fit. But frankly, we're nearly at the end of the Prosecution case here. This is evidence that we have been expecting for a long time. We have set up this evidence for a long time. We've tendered the military security rules to indicate, among other things -- and obviously at the end of the case we'll go to those military security rules to indicate the legal source of the undoubted competence of the military security to deal with crimes like this. That's part of that -- that's obviously we've put that to Mr. Eminovic and indeed to all of the military security people who have been in this court. But, Your Honours, it's just a matter of too much fundamental importance for the Prosecutor to now say they're withdrawing the witness and they don't have to tell you why. It's pretty obvious why, and now I invite Your Honours to consider the submissions I've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Chana, I give you three minutes for a very concise response, mainly concentrated on the three propositions put forward by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence have put forward three propositions. The first one is that they be -- essentially be allowed to cross-examine, and the Prosecution -- that position is not acceptable to the Prosecution that this witness is called. We do not lead evidence from this witness, thus allowing the Defence to cross-examine. Your Honour, I do not see the basis for such a proposal. If they want to lead evidence from this witness, they are entitled to call this witness as a Defence witness. So that is certainly not acceptable to the Prosecution in any manner or form. Equally, Your Honour, the option that we introduce the witness statement and the proofing notes 89(F) is equally not acceptable to the proposition -- acceptable to the Prosecution. We cannot be dictated by the Defence as to how we must conduct our case. It is our case, and when learned counsel makes a submission that we as the custodians of justice must make available all witnesses for the Defence, I find that a curious assertion because that is not the way trials at the Tribunal are run. It is an adversarial system. Each party may bring whichever witnesses they want, and if they feel that some witness is not going to assist them, then they are free not to call that witness, allowing the Defence to call that witness. Your Honour, in respect of the third proposal, is that this becomes a court witness. Now, Your Honour, I cannot say too much about that other than to -- this would be a matter for Your Honours to decide whether you would wish to call this witness, and Your Honours will then have to decide what would be the procedures to be put into place if Your Honours were so inclined to call this witness as a Court witness. From what I understand, the procedure would be that this witness is called, neither the Defence nor the Prosecution would be allowed to cross-examine but would only be allowed to ask leading questions -- non-leading questions from this witness. And of course Your Honours will question the witness to the extent Your Honours think it's desirable. Your Honours, while he was a military prosecutor, this man had absolutely no legal training whatsoever. He was not a Prosecutor in November 1993 he gives opinions, and those we -- the Prosecution feels are not relevant for the Prosecution case. We are not hiding anything here, Your Honour. The proofing notes have been -- and my learned counsel has accepted them to be extremely fair and transparent, but we do not wish to call that -- this witness. And we will not agree to any of the two proposals, Your Honour. And if Your Honours are so inclined to call this witness yourselves, of course the Prosecution in that event will leave the matter entirely in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I believe that at this moment, the Bench has to digest the submissions from the parties. We believe there is merits in the submissions from both parties, and we have to elaborate on that issue during the break. So we'll postpone our rulings on this very matter, and we'll continue the cross-examination of the present witness. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You still have some questions to ask, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Exactly. In my interest to speed up the proceedings, I feel that there are some questions I need to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, we won't object to leave being granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. I hope you do not open a new area and have another hour for this direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at most, four to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness H, I'm sure you were expecting to see Defence counsel. I just have one or two questions to ask you before I hand over. After the operation on the 14th of September, 1993, did you come to know about any killings of civilians during that operation, killings of Croat civilians during that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did find out about that a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it on Radio Rama, and this was something that soldiers were talking about. They also said they'd heard about it over Radio Rama, which is a local radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court what you heard or what the other soldiers heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there had been an operation and that some civilians had been killed in the village of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "civilians," are you referring to Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my last question, I'd like to go into private session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any cross-examination? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Guenael Mettraux and I appear as co-counsel for Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You have indicated in your evidence in-chief that in the relevant time, September 1993, you were a member of the Independent Prozor Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about the make-up of that battalion, its composition if you want. Is it correct that for a limited number of individuals, most members of the Independent Prozor Battalion came from the village of Here or surrounding hamlets. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most members of the battalion were from the village of Here, the village of Kute, and the village of Scipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those villages, sir, before the war were primarily inhabited by Bosnian Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those three villages which you've mentioned remain at all time under the control of the Bosnian government army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here fell on the 24th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: My question was imprecise, sir. I meant to say that until or until September 1993, those three villages had been or had remained under the control of the ABiH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in the summer of 1993, the Independent Prozor Battalion consisted mostly, if not exclusively, of non-professional soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In fact, sir, to your knowledge, was there any professional officer within the Independent Prozor Battalion at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Members of the Prozor Battalion were just like you, villagers who spontaneously took up arms at the beginning of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, you didn't wear any particular uniforms, and I mean members of the Independent Prozor Battalion, you would wear different outfits, pieces of clothing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you didn't wear any particular badges which would have identified you as members of the Independent Prozor Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the objection, but perhaps my learned friend can be precise about the time period when he's asking about the uniforms, because one of questions was: "Members of the Prozor Independent Battalion were just like you, villagers who spontaneously took up arms at the beginning of the conflict." Now beginning of the conflict is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I can make that clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, at -- in September of 1993, you didn't have any particular sort of uniform in the battalion; everyone was wearing different pieces of clothing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You essentially wore what you could find in terms of camouflage uniforms or sometimes had to wear your own civilian clothes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And at that time, again in September 1993, you did not wear -- you personally and other members of the Independent Prozor Battalion as far as you could tell did not wear any particular badge or insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I ask that we go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, are you also aware that at times, the civilian police would come to assist the army in the context of military operations, is that something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you aware of any civilian policemen taking part in the operation on Uzdol on the 14th of September, 1993, or is it something which is beyond your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I didn't see those civilian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like now, sir, to ask you a few questions about the situation on the ground as you saw it. Would it be correct to suggest that the Prozor area, which you were shown on various pictures earlier today, is a rather hilly environment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that on the hills of those -- on those -- on the slope of those hills are a number of villages, I mean villages would be dotting, if you want, the hills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, don't hesitate to correct me, sir. If there's anything left unsaid in that regard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what specifically you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll ask you this, then: In September of 1993, would it be correct to say that the ABiH, the Bosnian government army, controlled Here and the village -- and the villages around Here, that would be in September 1993, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army controlled the village of Here, the village of Kute, and the village of Scipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And on the other side the HVO would control, in September 1993 again, the village of Uzdol and the surrounding hamlets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would it also be correct to suggest that in between those two points, that is, between let's say Here and the school in Uzdol, there wasn't any clear front line like, for instance, the one that existed in Mostar at the time. Would it be a correct suggestion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the front line was pretty clear cut, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that front line was marked by a number of military outposts, wasn't it, HVO, ABiH outposts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But there were other places on that front line where villages would be sitting or where they would be directly exposed to the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would be the case with several of the villages which surrounded Uzdol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, would you know approximately how many HVO soldiers lived or operated in the area of Uzdol, a general number, if you can tell; if you can't, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was that there was a battalion. I'm not sure how they referred to the unit, but it should have been battalion strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And how many soldiers, sir, would make up a battalion, approximately again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would it be in the hundreds? In the dozens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well, sir. You also knew that civilians lived in the villages around Uzdol in September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that a number of HVO soldiers - and I ask you from your personal information - whether a number of HVO soldiers would go back to their homes at the end of their shift. Were you ware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that really is a speculative question. How is the witness supposed to answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because -- well, I'm not going into the details, but how could this witness know something on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, sir, was there any reconnaissance done of the area at the time which would have revealed the presence of HVO soldiers in houses? Is that something that you are aware of, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in no reconnaissance operations myself, but the assumption was there were soldiers staying there for the simple reason that most of the soldiers were natives of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. You've already indicated that on your way to the school in Cer, you didn't come across any civilians or, for that matters, any HVO soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Prior to going towards the school in Cer, you were aware at least of the possibility of coming across civilians, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. We just used the road where we were least likely to reveal our movements and our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I see. But you were aware, sir, that in case you came across civilians, you were not allowed to shoot at those civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we would have shot at them. We knew that civilians had nothing to do with it. We wouldn't have shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you also knew, sir, that you had an obligation, a legal obligation as a matter of fact, to distinguish between civilians and those involved in combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a rough idea, but there was no official order to that effect. It was a matter of personal moral responsibility, and it was based on that that I would never, under any conditions, have shot at a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, sir, those personal moral responsibility that you've just been mentioning, they are basics; you didn't need a reminder of that fact, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've indicated in your evidence in-chief that one of the tasks which you had been assigned as you went was to liberate Bosnian prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Was it your understanding at the time that the HVO kept Bosnian prisoners of war in or around the school in Cer; is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Was that your understanding at the time, sir, that Bosnian prisoners of war had been used by the HVO as human shield on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn, sir, to an aspect that you've discussed in your evidence in-chief, which was the amount of weaponry at the disposal of the HVO. You've discussed a tank close to the school in Cer and the fact that that tank was shelling the area of Here on the a daily basis. Was there also another tank, sir, at the time within the shooting range of Uzdol and Here, and I'm thinking of one, perhaps to help you, which was on the hill near the villages of Kranjcici and Osljani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the attack commenced, we realised there was tank fire being opened, we weren't sure from where. I think it was from the villages of Blace and Kranjcici.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Was it a single tank, sir, shelling your positions or was it two tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several tanks were firing at our positions. Throughout the operation on that day we only saw one, namely the one that was positioned in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you talk about shelling your positions, sir, you are talking about your positions as the attack went on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps the question is not very clear, sir. When you're talking about the tanks shelling your positions, you are talking about the positions in which you were at the time of the operation, in your case, Cer -- Uzdol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The witness has answered clearly and said that he only saw one tank on that day of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not asking about the sighting of any tank at this point, I'm asking about the shelling. The witness has indeed said he's seen only one tank, but he has said that another one was shelling the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean on the same day or on the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: On the same day, Your Honour. I can clarify this matter with the witness quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated that you saw only one tank on the 14th of September, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that tank was the tank which you've indicated earlier on the photograph which was shown to you, that is the tank that was near to the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is also correct, sir, that there was another tank on the hill near the village of Kranjcici which was shelling the village of Uzdol on the 14th of September, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Were you also aware of the HVO shelling the village of Uzdol or the general area around Uzdol with mortar fire, sir? Is that something you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What about the howitzer gun, sir, did the HVO make use of that howitzer to try to repel your attack on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they used both Howitzers and multiple rocket launchers as well as tank fire and mortars. I think they used all of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And was the shelling on that day, sir, on the 14th of September, was it constant or was it sporadic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more constant than sporadic, especially as our units were pulling out of the village. While the units were pulling out, they kept pounding away.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in addition to heavy weapons, were you aware of being shot at from small arm weapons? Is that something you became aware of while you were in the village of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, being a military man, or being in the army, let's say, at the time, had you how precisely could a mortar or tank -- let me put it the other way, perhaps. How effective, sir, according to you, would, let's say, a tank or a mortar be to target a running soldier? Would a tank or a mortar be an effective weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. I -- this witness is indeed -- was a part of the military, but that question is a very specific question which requires specific expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this witness is a soldier. He may answer this question so far as he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask the question again. In your experience, and having been a soldier for a number of years, how effective would be -- would a tank or mortar fire be in targeting, let's say, a running soldier? How effective would that be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the chances of hitting the soldier would be extremely small.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What about 100 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be much easier to target.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What about 100 soldiers in inhabited areas, in villages? How easy would that be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I raise the same objection. We're now getting into a specific knowledge of artillery and mortars, and there are many types of mortars. I can't see how the witness can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's kind of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this witness was on the fire at the time, and if my learned friend wants me to ask the question specifically in relation to the village of Uzdol, I'm more than happy to do so. And indeed I can do so if Your Honour requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, on the 14th of September, 1993, you've indicated that you were under constant heavy fighting -- heavy shelling, I'm sorry, and heavy shooting from the HVO side --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
